content.text: An animate aria is the spirit of music in physical form. Granted life through magic and ceremony, these constructs emanate the inspiring music used to create them, usually acting as expensive and entertaining decor for the wealthy elite as well as simple servants and guardians.

As a construct of sound, an aria is usually heard and not seen, though it does have a physical body: a large humanoid-shaped framework without any distinguishing physical features, approximately 12 feet tall, made up of stylized symbols of musical notation. It can completely suppress its natural invisibility if needed, and while its musical aura can't be fully silenced, it can be reduced to a pleasant indoor volume suitable for light entertainment. The music used in the ritual to created an animate aria is the only sound that the construct can emit. It doesn't have the creative spark to create new music, though an animate aria in distress can emit all of the measures of its song at once to create a painful and deafening discordance. When it does so, the musical notation that makes up an animate aria's visible form briefly becomes jagged and broken, making the construct easier to see.

Animate arias are especially vulnerable to magic with sonic and silencing effects, which disrupt the melody that sustains them. When subjected to such effects, the extremities of the construct's shape begin to fade away, starting with its hands and feet. Those who create and maintain animate arias refer to this development as "diminishing."
An animate aria can use its hearing as a precise sense at the listed range.

The striking image of the cephalophix's head resting in their hands is enough to give any mortal pause, but the horrifying shrieks and splattering black tar that spray from their mouths is disturbing to even other devils. Cephalophixes hate all magic with passion and fury, and they especially loathe divine magic, believing it to be the gods' unfair finger on the scales of planar conflict. The irony that they require magic to combat it isn't lost on them, but they aren't above any method that leads to the death of another magic user. Their hatred of all magic makes it difficult for other devils to work with cephalophixes, and more powerful devils usually keep them in soundproof cages until they're needed. Cephalophixes prefer this arrangement as well, meditating in solitude far from the magic and its users that they despise.

Cerberuses are flayed, fiendish, three-headed watchdogs of Hell. Their bodies bulge with furless, blood-soaked muscle and sinew, and their eyes churn with hellfire. Three massive heads each display a set of razor-sharp teeth, which carry a curse that prevents their prey from escaping even to other planes. These cruel hounds delight in malice, their sadistic cunning perfectly suiting them for tracking, trapping, and eviscerating the damned and the undead. When a cerberus has their scent, neither can escape from the beast's relentless tracking.

While cerberuses form matriarchal packs in the wilds of the unholy planes, they can understand Diabolic and will take instruction from any they sufficiently respect or fear. This loyalty means they're often put to work as infernal guardians, trackers, and enforcers of their masters' will. While not as clever as most humanoids, cerberuses have a cunning that the foolish might dismiss. These fiendish hounds are fully capable of devising and executing complex plans—often leading to the demise of incautious masters.

As mortals persevere against the predations and schemes of the denizens of the unholy planes—daemons, demons, devils, and the like—such fiends are driven to fury, and a desire for vengeance against mortals rises in their collective wills. Erinyes are those emotions made manifest. While not as ancient as some of their extraplanar counterparts, erinyes have existed for as long as mortals have fought back against fiends. An erinys's form mocks mortals' frailty: a humanoid shape with wings as black as pitch and eyes that glow with baleful fire. Fiendish vipers slither constantly across their skin and through their hair, and an erinys can form these snakes into a living whip or direct them to bite anyone who draws too near. Most erinyes wear deep black robes or armor.

Erinyes can be found wherever unholy fiends feel a strong desire for vengeance. Erinyes consider themselves mercenaries, working for whatever fiendish faction gives them the opportunity to vent their wrath on mortals. They can be found throughout the unholy planes and the Universe. Rarely, an erinys will make a deal with a mortal to perform acts of vengeance on that mortal's behalf, especially if those acts are particularly violent.

If an erinys ever drops or is disarmed of their scourge of snakes, the scourge discorporates into a tangle of fiendish vipers that immediately returns to the erinys. The erinys can reform a discorporated scourge of snakes with an Interact action, but they can never have more than one scourge of snakes at a time.

While Hellknights are widely feared and usually respected, most joined due to their sense of duty and their wish to be a part of a greater whole, working to bring forth a world where laws and order rule.

The word "Hellknight" is enough to strike fear into even the most seasoned of veterans. When even one Hellknight enters a town, many cower in their homes, praying that the feared soldier has no business with them. Hellknights are easily identified by their unique armor, among the most iconic in all of Golarion. Decorated with fearsome adornments, the individual Hellknight's goals are clear since those enhancements are the very things that identify their order. Donning this armor without the title of Hellknight is a foolish endeavor, as the punishment for doing so will often yield a fate worse than death.

Joining the ranks of the Hellknights is no small matter either. A trial by fire is an understatement, for they must best a devil in a duel, and their victory must be witnessed by a Hellknight in good standing. Once initiated, the requirement for Hellknights of all orders is to steadfastly uphold the Measure and the Chain, a two-faceted approach to their edicts. The Measure is a series of laws that the Hellknights believe all humanoids should adhere. The Chain is the three-pronged approach that they take to enforce the Measure: order, discipline, and mercilessness. The laws within the Measure and how they focus on them through the lens of the Chain is how Hellknights have earned their fearsome reputation.

The average Hellknights' most distinguishing piece of apparel is their fearsome plate armor, but the signifer's most infamous attire is their mask. The signifer's mask, notable for its lack of eyeholes, renders the wearer incognito while still evoking fear in their enemies. Unlike other Hellknights, signifers rely on more than physical might, instead blending powerful magic to augment their abilities or wrack their opponents' minds. Through using spells with mental effects to break their opponents' resolves or by summoning unholy creatures to their sides to bolster their numbers, signifers manipulate the battlefield in unique ways.

Kophoses are pain purists who believe that screams and tears detract from the experience of suffering. These velstracs gouge out their eyes and cut out their tongues to make such outbursts impossible, covering the empty cavities with patches of their own skin or spiked lumps of metal, though they are still disturbingly able to see and speak. Beyond these self-inflicted injuries, they resemble typical humans, though their bodies are covered in countless gashes and scars that slowly, gruesomely heal themselves. They wrap themselves in dozens of barbed chains.

Kophoses consider it their purpose to find mortals who either inflict physical suffering on others or who are plagued with constant pain due to medical conditions and teach them how to be silent and stoic in their agony.

This massive collection of bone-white branches and blood-matted fur stalks the grove it protects with relentless dedication, hunting down trespassers and delivering retribution at its creator's command with brutal efficiency. These fetid guardians are created in a bloody ritual using the twigs of a dying plant and the fur of a rabid animal and are given life with the sacrifice of an intelligent creature. They're usually seen at the side of corrupted druids, keeping their sanctums safe from trespassers. Other druids or rangers might stomach the gruesome ritual if they find themselves desperate enough to need protection at any cost.

These twisted constructs are almost undetectable in the wild despite their prodigious size, gliding invisibly between the trees. The unnatural growth that surrounds an effigy at all times gives its presence away—but by the time the vines wrap around an intruder's legs, it's far too late to escape the creature's wrath. Without warning, the effigy then emerges from the soil in an explosion of rocks and wood splinters, carving a bloody path through its enemies. Effigies often leave a single obvious escape route when they attack, forcing their prey to delve deeper into the woods where more of their kind lie in wait.

Munagolas are some of the most feared fiendish warriors in Hell, for they combine the aerial strength and craftiness of erinyes with sheer brute force rivaling that of the strongest devils. The first munagola was forged by Eiseth, Hell's Valkyrie, from the flesh of other devils. The process took centuries but resulted in a loyal soldier to rival her own rage and might. Since she established her realm in Dis, Eiseth has created armies of executioner devils to serve her will.

Munagolas are vicious combatants, empowered by their fury and growing stronger with each successful blow, but their true strength lies in their commanding presence on the battlefield. They often lead troops of other flying devils from the front, driving them to faster and deadlier assaults that leave the enemies of their queen with no chance to respond.

Munagolas and erinyes who serve Eiseth work well together, though a few munagolas hold contempt for the members of the Golden Company, believing their ostentatious armor to belittle the glory of battle. However, even such devils can't argue with the Golden Company's results.

A creature with greater darkvision can see perfectly well in areas of darkness and dim light, though such vision is in black and white only. A creature with greater darkvision can see through even forms of magical darkness.

A monster with telepathy can communicate mentally with any creatures within the listed radius, as long as they share a language. This doesn't give any special access to their thoughts, and communicates no more information than normal speech would.

A shadowbound creature can assume a shadowy form. In this state, the creature gains the incorporeal trait. It has resistance 10 to all damage (except force, ghost touch, spirit, or vitality; double resistance vs. non-magical), is immune to precision damage, and can't use any actions with the attack or manipulate trait. The shadowbound creature can Dismiss this effect to become solid again, but if it does so in an area of bright light, it's Stunned 1 for 1 round.

Where there is one strix hunter, more likely lie in wait. Strix hunters rely on practiced coordination with their kin, spending many hours training until their maneuvers seamlessly link together. This allows hunters to unleash a barrage of attacks while staying on the move and rapidly trading positions in battle. While strix hunters might train in groups of a dozen or more, a hunting party on the prowl is typically made up of no more than six individuals. These hunters interchange roles and have no set leader, with each member calling the shots in a loose rotation. This communal decision-making style shines when facing intelligent foes, baffling opponents who might normally rely on targeting a leader to break formation and morale.

Whether they fight together or alone, strix hunters rely on their ability to swoop in and out of melee while quickly changing weapons to disorient their enemies and keep them from finding any one tactic to fight back. The coordinated flurry of arrows, blades, and talons a strix hunting party can deliver is usually devastating to their prey. If the victim should live through it, they are left reeling.

Strix hunters rarely take trophies from their kills, as they consider the use of their martial skills to be practical elements of survival—whether they are hunting for food or driving off unwanted intruders.
The strix hunter Strides or Flies once, then Interacts to swap weapons.
The strix hunter Flies downward up to twice their Speed and then makes a Strike. If the Strike hits and the hunter moved at least 20 feet downward, the hunter attempts to Demoralize the target.

The strix hunter makes a ranged Strike against their prey, and a single ally within 30 feet can use their reaction to make a Strike against the same target. If both attacks hit, the target is Off-Guard until the start of the hunter's next turn.

The strix hunter designates a single creature they can see and hear, or one they're Tracking, as their prey. The hunter gains a +2 circumstance bonus to Perception checks to Seek the prey and to Survival checks to Track the prey. The first time the hunter hits their prey in a round, they deal an additional 1d8 precision damage. These effects last until the hunter uses Stalk Prey again.

Umbral shepherds are often brought to Golarion by shadowcallers, where they serve as spies, puppeteers, and manipulators for the glory of Zon-Kuthon. Unwavering in their obedience to their lord, these entities ruthlessly possess mortal hosts to carry out their master's will.

The bond created by a shepherd's parasitic possession is antithetical to life. As the shepherd sustains themself with a mortal form, they drag the host's body toward its doom. This degeneration also risks the shepherd's existence, which depends on the host's continued life, so they must find a new host before the last fully succumbs. Those tracking an umbral shepherd often do so by following the trail of desperate and broken hosts this process leaves behind. The trail is rarely random. The shepherd is drawn toward the goal set by their divine master; it is often possible to identify a shepherd's next target if their ultimate goal is understood.

Despite this determination, a cornered shepherd is not above choosing targets of opportunity. If one of these parasites identifies its pursuers, its favorite tactic is to isolate the most vulnerable of the group and possess them, providing false leads or alerting allies to delay and even kill the rest of the hunting party.

In the Netherworld, umbral shepherds naturally resemble humanoid figures with an ashen torso and a twisted demonic face. No two shepherds are truly alike except for their lack of visible limbs; some bear marks of torture and open wounds, while others possess features that are more diabolic than demonic. They can also manipulate their own essence to manifest shadowy tendrils, burrowing bloodlessly through flesh with gruesome ease as their vile rot infects surrounding tissue.

This has the same effect as the possession spell (DC 22) with an unlimited duration, except they aren't Unconscious and aren't Paralyzed when the effect ends, though they are killed if host dies. A creature possessed by an umbral shepherd applies shadowy sublimation to all its Strikes and is Doomed 1. For each consecutive month the shepherd possesses the creature, the doomed value increases by 1, to a maximum of 4.

Yzobus are herd beasts common across northern plains and mountains, resembling a cross between a steer, a sturdy horse, and a yak. They most notably feature a pungent stench caused by bodily secretions building up within their thick, shaggy pelts-a stench so strong that yzobu herds can often be smelled before they appear. Territorial and aggressive, yzobus often attack other creatures on sight. When threatened, a herd launches into a stampede, trampling any in their path and goring survivors with their distinctive horns.

Some ranchers trade yzobu hides as a workable leather for mercenaries and guards, but the powerful smell means that most ranchers tend their small herds on the outskirts of towns. Typically, yzobus aren't raised to a specific age, but rather are killed whenever one escapes and poses a threat. The hides require an intensive tanning process with almost constant brushing and hours soaking in salt water-but the effort results in a leather both soft to the touch and sturdy enough to work as an effective armor for several years.
Hides aren't the only yzobu products worth harvesting. A female yzobu's milk is rich and nutrient-rich, making it a staple food source in some regions. Their meat is less enticing but still edible.

These beasts remain a permanent part of hobgoblin society, where their aggressive temperaments and durable, sturdy bodies are great assets. Hobgoblins possess an immunity to yzobu stench, and they view the fact that other races sickened by it as further evidence of their own superiority. They also highly prize yzobu mounts, and hobgoblin commanders often paint their yzobu's horns in varying colors and patterns to show how many enemies the mount has killed. Yzobu cavalry are a staple of hobgoblin military action, and they played a key role in the recent Ironfang Invasion that led to the formation of the new hobgoblin nation of Oprak in Avistan. The establishment of Oprak meant that many Avistani who had never encountered yzobus before have grown familiar-if not enchanted-with their distinctive odor.
